title: Sleep and the athlete: narrative review and 2021 expert consensus recommendations
authors: Walsh NP, Halson SL, Sargent C, Roach GD, Nédélec M, Gupta L, Leeder J, Fullagar HH, et al.
population: Athletes (narrative review and expert consensus; abstract emphasises elite athletes)
findings: Elite athletes are particularly susceptible to sleep inadequacies: habitual short sleep (<7 hours/night) and poor sleep quality (for example fragmentation).
Performance is reduced by a night or more without sleep, but the influence of partial restriction over 1-3 nights remains unclear.
In the wider population, habitually sleeping <7 hours/night increases susceptibility to respiratory infection.
Sleep is influenced by sport-specific factors (training, travel, competition) and non-sport factors (for example female gender, stress, anxiety).

A one-size-fits-all recommendation (for example 7-9 hours/night) is unlikely to be ideal; an individualised approach considering perceived sleep need is recommended; research is needed on napping and sleep extension.
limitations: Studies in athletes often have inadequate experimental control, few females, and questionable sleep-assessment validity; no quantitative load-adjustment rules.
implications: Use sleep as a risk modifier: when habitual sleep is below about 7 h over several nights, surface a warning and an option to reduce intensity, not an automatic large volume cut.
Do not penalise a single short night; act on multi-night patterns and the athlete's perceived sleep need.
Ask for perceived sleep quality and let the athlete set a personal sleep need.
